report:
## Report

The evidence, though not high-quality, does lean toward "yes"—honey appears to help ease acute cough symptoms in children older than 12 months.

The most authoritative source is the Cochrane systematic review (Oduwole et al., 2018, updated 2023), which pooled randomized controlled trials comparing honey to placebo, no treatment, diphenhydramine, or salbutamol in children aged 1–18 with acute upper respiratory infection-related cough. It found that honey likely reduces cough frequency and severity better than placebo/no treatment, and possibly outperforms some over-the-counter cough medicines, with children recovering symptoms slightly sooner. However, the certainty of evidence was rated **low to very low** due to small trial sizes, heterogeneity in outcome measurement, and risk of bias (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children; https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007094.pub5/full).

A 2023 independent systematic review reached a similar conclusion, calling honey "more effective than placebo/no treatment or cough medications" for symptom relief and improved sleep in children, again with low-quality evidence (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10570220/). A widely cited placebo-controlled AAP-published trial (Cohen et al., Pediatrics 2012) also found a single nighttime dose of honey reduced nocturnal cough and improved sleep for children and parents compared with placebo (https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/130/3/465/30142/Effect-of-Honey-on-Nocturnal-Cough-and-Sleep).

Important caveat: honey must never be given to infants under 12 months due to infant botulism risk (https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/honey-botulism.html).

**Bottom line:** For children over one year, honey probably modestly relieves acute cough and improves sleep better than no treatment or some medications, but the evidence base remains limited and larger, higher-quality trials are needed.
